title: Plain bread, hungry
hookLine: arriving late and tired, Seneca finds dry bread delicious (Letters 123)

lines: GAS STATION CRACKERS AFTER A HIKE.
cards: Gas station crackers after a long hike. Cold toast after a night in a hospital waiting room. Instant noodles at two in the morning after a move.

Meals like these can taste better than they have any right to. Letter 123 opens with Seneca reaching his country house in the Alban hills, late at night, worn out from a trip that was more uncomfortable than long.
Nothing is ready, he says, except himself. The baker has no bread.

teach.b: First, nothing is ready, and that's fine. Seneca lies down to rest and lets the cook and the baker take their time. Nothing is heavy, he says, if you take it calmly; nothing is worth anger that you can simply wait out.
A tired man in a dark house decides not to make it worse. Second, the bread. The baker has none, so someone finds some: the steward, the doorkeeper, a tenant.
It's coarse and dry. Bad bread, someone might protest.

teach.h: DRY BREAD: WAIT, HUNGER WILL SOFTEN IT.
teach.b: Wait, Seneca answers, it'll get better; hunger will make it soft. So he decides he won't eat until he either has good bread or stops turning up his nose at the bad. Third, hunger as the seasoning.
The idea is older than Seneca.
The Roman writer Cicero passes on a saying of Socrates: hunger is the seasoning of food, and thirst of drink. Seneca adds his own rule: don't eat until your stomach asks. Fourth, what this is for.
Not a plan to starve yourself, and not a lecture against good food. Seneca's point is freedom.
Someone who can only be happy with fresh bread is hostage to every baker. Someone who's learned that plain bread tastes fine when you're truly hungry can arrive late, anywhere, and be content.
The sauce was the hunger, and he brought it with him.

how: Some people practicing Stoic simplicity occasionally eat plain food and wait for real hunger before meals, to learn that contentment doesn't depend on fine things.

coarse bread made good enough by real hunger
a simple loaf the poor ate every single day

games.q: you're Seneca, late at your country house. the only bread is coarse and dry. what do you do?
o: send someone to the city for fresh bread.
wait a little; hunger will make it good.
go to bed angry and hungry.
games.why: he says hunger will make the bread soft, and decides to wait until it does.

practice: Check in with your body right now: are you really hungry, on a scale of one to ten, or do you often eat before the number climbs, out of habit or the clock?

Picture your next meal as the simplest version of itself, bread, rice, fruit, and imagine tasting the first bite with real hunger. If you have any health reason not to wait, simply notice the hunger without testing it.

wordCard.voice: Plain bread. Coarse, dry, found by a doorkeeper late at night, and good enough, Seneca says, once hunger has done its work. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'hunger': in Cicero's version of Socrates' saying, the seasoning of food.

carryVoice: Your line: hunger is the sauce. Whoever brings the hunger is free of every baker. That's day four hundred eighty-nine.
